haiku-low.q1: They see the generic message: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
haiku-low.q2: They get the same generic message and nothing is sent. The hourly limit is 3 per account, counted from reset_tokens rows.
haiku-low.q3: A link lasts 30 minutes from issue. A newer request or a successful password save ends it sooner.
haiku-low.q4: The link stays live and unused, so the user can retry until it expires. It is marked used only when the password saves.
haiku-low.q5: No devices stay logged in, because all of the user's sessions are deleted, including the one used for the reset. The user must log in again with the new password.
haiku-low.q6: The queue failure is logged and the row stays. The worker retries 3 times, then drops the job. The user is not told; they can request a new link within the hourly limit.
haiku-low.q7: The server generates the raw token, stores only its hash, and puts the raw token in the link inside the queued email job.
haiku-low.q8: It hashes the token from the URL and looks up the reset_tokens row by that hash. It then checks the row is unused and unexpired.
haiku-low.q9: It is the count of the account's reset_tokens rows created in the last hour in Postgres. Rows are never deleted, so old ones age out of the one-hour window.
haiku-low.q10: When a new link is issued, the account's live links are marked used, in the same transaction that inserts the new row.
haiku-low.q11: Marking the link used, saving the password hash, and deleting all sessions happen in one transaction. The password-changed email is queued after that.
haiku-low.q12: The conditional update (used = false and expiry > now) lets only one succeed. The second changes 0 rows, rolls back, and shows the expired page.

sonnet.q1: They see the generic message: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
sonnet.q2: Step 1 counts the account's reset_tokens rows from the last hour. Three or more means it stops, shows the generic message, and sends nothing.
sonnet.q3: 30 minutes from issue. It ends sooner if the link is marked used (successful password save), or if a newer request marks the account's live links used.
sonnet.q4: Still live (unused). An error is shown and the user can retry until it expires.
sonnet.q5: None. All of the user's sessions are deleted, including the device doing the reset. There is no automatic login, so the user is redirected to the login page and logs in with the new password.
sonnet.q6: NOT STATED for the provider rejecting it directly. For delivery failures in general, the worker retries 3 times with backoff, then logs and drops the job. Nobody is told. The user can request a new link within the hourly limit.
sonnet.q7: The raw token is generated at request time and put into the link inside the "send reset email" job on the Email queue. The queue and worker then send it. The raw token is never stored in the database.
sonnet.q8: The server hashes the token from the URL (SHA-256) and finds the reset_tokens row by that hash. The link is good if the row exists, is unused and is not expired. Otherwise it shows the "expired" page.
sonnet.q9: In Postgres, by counting the account's reset_tokens rows created in the last hour. The window is rolling, so rows age out of the count after an hour. Rows are never deleted.
sonnet.q10: In step 1, in the same transaction that inserts the new row, the account's live links are marked used. Those killed rows still count toward the hourly limit.
sonnet.q11: One transaction: mark the link used (conditional update), save the new password hash, and delete all of the user's sessions. The "password changed" email job is queued after that transaction, and a queue failure is only logged.
sonnet.q12: The conditional update (where id = row and used = false and expiry > now) inside the transaction. The first submit updates 1 row. The second updates 0 rows, rolls back and shows the "expired" page.
